extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, PTAB practitioners, and IP counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and discretionary factors the PTAB applies when deciding institution, joinder, discovery, rehearing, service, and related procedural issues in IPR/PGR proceedings, including objective indicia of non-obviousness and overlap-with-parallel-litigation considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations as objective indicia of non-obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary considerations such as commercial success, long-felt need, and industry praise can weigh against a finding of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board may find claims non-obvious based on secondary considerations after otherwise finding prior-art grounds sufficient. Evidence must show nexus to the claimed invention (see 'coextensive' product or direct result of limitations). Petitioner must meaningfully rebut by, e.g., laying out timing of advertising/marketing and explaining how marketing—not claimed features—caused success. (Cases: Biotechnologies S.A. v. Novo Nordisk; Yita LLC v. MacNeil IP LLC; Ontel Prods. Corp. v. Guy A. Shaked Invs. Ltd.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of nexus when commercial product is coextensive with claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patent owner's commercial product is coextensive with the claims, a presumption of nexus to commercial success arises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When coextensiveness is shown, nexus is presumed; Petitioner can attempt to rebut by showing success due to non-claimed factors (e.g., marketing), but must present timing/details. Board may decline to reach coextensiveness if nexus shown via direct causal link between praise/acceptance and claimed limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry praise and acceptance as nexus evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Industry praise and acceptance may serve as objective indicia of non-obviousness if shown to be the direct result of claimed limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unrebutted testimony that industry praise is directly caused by claimed subject matter can satisfy nexus without requiring a coextensive product showing. Board found such evidence persuasive to defeat obviousness challenges. (Ontel Prods. case)

rubrics_metrics.name: Fintiv discretionary-denial factors (parallel litigation considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: When parallel district-court litigation exists, the Board may exercise discretion under §314(a) (Fintiv) to deny institution by weighing factors such as the scheduled trial date relative to the final written decision, whether a stay was denied, and the stage of the district-court case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key considerations: whether trial is scheduled before PTAB's final written decision (and how far in advance), whether a stay motion was denied, whether invalidity expert reports have been served, and whether petitioner took dilatory actions (e.g., late filings). A short trial gap weighs against institution; median time-to-trial statistics may be considered to assess the actual expected trial date. Petitioner stipulations (Sand Revolution or Sotera-type) affect the analysis; broad stipulations that leave open related references weaken their value. (F5 Networks, Hillman Group, Apple v. XR Comms.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Compelling evidence of unpatentability precludes Fintiv denial (Director guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Per Director Vidal's guidance, the Board will not rely on Fintiv factors to deny institution where a petition presents compelling evidence of unpatentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Petitioner presents compelling unpatentability evidence at institution stage (i.e., strong prima facie case), the Board may decline to exercise discretion to deny institution despite parallel litigation. (STMicroelectronics v. Trustees of Purdue Univ.; Hewlett Packard v. BillJCo.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Sotera-type stipulations and their weight in Fintiv analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Sotera-style stipulations (promises to avoid overlap with district-court invalidity positions) can weigh against discretionary denial—even if the stipulation was served but not filed in district court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board has credited Sotera stipulations when offered in IPR (even if not filed in district court), treating a stipulation filed as an exhibit in the IPR as a representation subject to 37 C.F.R. § 42.11(c) and sanctions for non-compliance. A Sotera stipulation alone can preclude discretionary denial under Director guidance. (Ecofasten Solar; RideCo; other cited decisions)

rubrics_metrics.name: General Plastic factors for denying follow-on petitions/joinders
rubrics_metrics.description: Under General Plastic, the Board may deny institution of follow-on petitions when multiple petitions present substantially similar grounds and a 'significant relationship' exists between petitioners or proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors include overlap of grounds and prior art, whether a later petitioner had a significant relationship with earlier petitioner(s), and whether later petitions raise unique challenges. The Board has denied institution where the later petition substantially duplicated an earlier one and significant relationship/overlap existed. Conversely, lack of significant relationship (no co-defendant status, different products, or additional claims) supports institution. (Home Depot v. Link Labs; Samsung v. Scramoge Tech.; Intel v. VLSI)

rubrics_metrics.name: No per se bar to copycat or 'me-too' petitions; copying alone not 'significant relationship'
rubrics_metrics.description: Copying an earlier petition to satisfy joinder requirements does not alone create a 'significant relationship' for General Plastic purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board has recognized that copying previously-instituted petitions is common and does not automatically warrant discretionary denial under General Plastic. The broader context (number of accused entities, relationships between parties, whether the later petitioner would simply be an understudy) determines the result. (SAP Am. v. Express Mobile; Intel joinder decisions)

rubrics_metrics.name: Joinder institution decisions are binary (no conditional institution)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board's decision to institute review is binary—either institute or not—and it will not make conditional institution decisions tied to hypothetical future events (e.g., petitioner withdrawing if lead petitioner withdraws).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board will not rule on conditional scenarios not before it and denied requests to attach conditions to joinder institution. (STMicroelectronics v. Ocean Semiconductor)

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion for additional discovery – interests of justice standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioners seeking additional discovery under the 'interests of justice' standard must show factors such as possession of the requested information, that the requested discovery is likely to yield useful information (more than mere possibility), and inability to obtain equivalent information by other means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board may grant additional discovery when petitioners already possess the requested documents, can show the discovery is likely useful (not mere allegation), and cannot generate equivalent information by other methods. The Board may decline to address whether discovery is 'routine' when additional-discovery criteria are satisfied. (TCL Indus. v. ParkerVision)

rubrics_metrics.name: Service requirements for petitions (35 U.S.C. §321(c) and 37 C.F.R. §42.205)
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition must satisfy statutory service requirements; electronic service is valid only 'upon agreement of the parties' under 37 C.F.R. §42.205(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emailing a petition to counsel within the statutory window is insufficient absent agreement to electronic service; physical service (e.g., USPS) remains a key method to satisfy the service requirement. Failure to timely serve can render a petition untimely under the nine-month statutory window. (IronRidge v. Pegasus Solar)

rubrics_metrics.name: 325(d) denial where arguments previously considered by the Office
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 325(d) may support denial of a petition when the written-description (or other) arguments are the same or substantially the same as arguments the Office previously considered during prosecution and Petitioner has not shown that the Examiner materially erred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board will deny institution under §325(d) when Petition's arguments match those considered in a sibling application examined by the same examiner at the same time, unless Petitioner demonstrates material error by the Examiner. (Guardant Health v. Univ. of Washington)

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness prevents reaching merits on patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: If claims are indefinite such that the Board cannot ascertain their scope with reasonable certainty, the Board will not make an unpatentability determination on the merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying district-court constructions may lead the Board to find claims indefinite; in that circumstance, PTAB cannot evaluate patentability of claims. (Micron Tech. v. Unification Techs.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion to strike – new theory/evidence and prejudice test
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion to strike reply arguments may be denied if the reply does not cite new evidence or point to different prior-art components and the patent owner is not prejudiced by addressing the reply in a sur-reply without expert rebuttal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board considers whether reply raised wholly new theories or evidence that could not have been anticipated; mere new emphasis on existing arguments is often permitted. Failure to show prejudice or introduction of new evidence weighs against striking. (TCL Indus. v. ParkerVision)

rubrics_metrics.name: Recusal standards for APJs
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative Patent Judges are governed by the Standards of Ethical Conduct for Employees of the Executive Branch, not the Model Code of Judicial Conduct; recusal requires a showing of a disqualifying financial interest or other applicable ground under those standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that the USPTO/PTAB are biased because of alleged patent infringement by the Office are insufficient absent proof that the proceeding implicates a financial interest of APJs or the government that would affect impartiality. Arguments based on incorrect standards will be rejected. (Google LLC v. Defenders of the American Dream)

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial for premature IPR filing when PGR pending or AIA-eligibility unresolved
rubrics_metrics.description: An IPR petition filed prematurely (e.g., when the patent is an AIA patent for which no IPR may be filed until nine months after issuance) may be denied as untimely or ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the Board determines the patent is an AIA patent and the IPR was filed within the statutory window disallowing IPRs, the Board will deny the IPR petition as ineligible. (Apple v. MemoryWeb)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of median time-to-trial statistics in Fintiv factor 2
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may present district-court median time-to-trial statistics for the Board's consideration when evaluating whether the parallel-court trial date weighs against institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board can apply the district's median time-to-trial to the currently scheduled trial date to assess whether the trial will actually occur before PTAB's final written decision; this assessment can change the weight of Fintiv factor 2. (Apple v. XR Comms.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretionary denial when district court finds claims ineligible under §101
rubrics_metrics.description: A district-court §101 invalidity finding can support discretionary denial based on efficiency, but the Board recognizes Fintiv is focused on §102/103 overlap and may analyze efficiency on other grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board may be reluctant to institute when efficiency strongly favors denial due to a district court's §101 decision, but it will explain that Fintiv specifically targets duplication of efforts for 102/103 issues. The Board evaluates whether institution would waste resources. (AviaGames v. Skillz Platform)

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial of rehearing for late-submitted evidence or late-developed stipulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board will deny rehearing requests that introduce evidence or stipulations after institution without showing good cause for late submission; evidence predating the institution decision but submitted late may be expunged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioner must request a conference or show good cause before submitting new evidence; post-institution stipulations offered without explanation as to lateness are unlikely to be credited. (Palo Alto Networks v. Centripetal; NXP USA v. Impinj)

rubrics_metrics.name: ITC proceedings generally do not justify Fintiv denial
rubrics_metrics.description: Parallel ITC proceedings are not a basis for discretionary denial under Fintiv because the ITC lacks authority to invalidate patents and its rulings are not binding on the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments seeking denial based on a parallel ITC proceeding (to avoid duplicative effort) are unpersuasive because ITC invalidity rulings are not binding on the USPTO or district courts. (Unified Patents v. Causam Enterprises)

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial of joinder when joinder petitioner would assume leading role or substantially similar grounds previously denied
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may deny a joinder petition when the joinder petitioner would not act as an understudy but immediately assume a lead role, when substantially similar grounds were previously denied, or where a jury has already decided validity against the petitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors include whether the lead petitioner has settled (leaving the joinder petitioner to lead), similarity to previously-denied petitions, lack of stipulations to reduce overlap, and the existence of a jury trial finding against invalidity. (Code200 v. Bright Data)

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignor-estoppel limitation does not bar assignor from filing an IPR
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignor estoppel does not automatically preclude an assignor (former inventor/assignor) from filing an IPR petition against the assigned patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where an inventor signed a declaration as original inventor and later worked for a petitioner accused of infringement, the Board has indicated assignor estoppel is not an absolute bar to filing an IPR; specifics may depend on factual circumstances (discussion cut off in source).
